subject_line: The catalog cards in City of Incurable Women
email_body:
Dear Maud,

In City of Incurable Women, the short linked pieces about the women of the Salpêtrière sit between case notes, period photographs and catalog cards, and some of that archival text is drawn from real sources while some is invented. I would love to ask how you decided where the documents should stop and your own imagining of women like Avril Jane should begin.

The Author Ledger is an independent project featuring short Author Spotlights. Each portrait is built from a few written questions, which you can answer at your own pace, and the full text is shared with you for review before publication.

Would you be open to taking part? No pressure either way.

Best regards,
The Author Ledger
hook_note: City of Incurable Women (Bellevue Literary Press, 2022) mixes linked prose with case notes, Salpêtrière photographs and catalog cards, partly from primary sources, partly invented (Boston Globe, HNS); UMD English professor; email seen in search result (UMD faculty directory).

subject_line: A missing brother in post-Franco Spain
email_body:
Dear Gabrielle,

The Sleeping World follows a young woman searching for her missing brother in Spain just after Franco, a moment when the country itself was unsure what it was waking into. I am curious how you found your way into that particular period, and whether the private search and the political transition grew together in the drafting or one came first.

The Author Ledger is an independent project featuring short Author Spotlights. Each portrait is built from a few written questions, which you can answer at your own pace, and the full text is shared with you for review before publication. I would also be glad to touch on Are We Ever Our Own.

Would you be open to taking part? No pressure either way.

Best regards,
The Author Ledger
hook_note: UMD faculty page describes The Sleeping World as a young woman searching for her missing brother in post-Franco Spain, plus story collection Are We Ever Our Own; email seen in search result (UMD faculty directory).

subject_line: Jamaica, Puerto Rico and Makeshift Altar
email_body:
Dear Amy,

Makeshift Altar works through migration, ancestry and belonging by way of both your Jamaican and Puerto Rican heritage, and it went on to win the American Book Award and the first CARICON Prize for Poetry. I would like to ask what the altar of the title is to you, and how you kept two family lines in conversation across a single debut collection.

The Author Ledger is an independent project featuring short Author Spotlights. Each portrait is built from a few written questions, which you can answer at your own pace, and the full text is shared with you for review before publication.

Would you be open to taking part? No pressure either way.

Best regards,
The Author Ledger
hook_note: Makeshift Altar (Univ. Press of Kentucky, 2024) on Jamaican/Puerto Rican heritage; won 2025 American Book Award and inaugural CARICON Prize (UK news, BC News); now at Boston College Messina College; email seen in search result (BC faculty directory).
